title: What If You Fell Into Jupiter? You'd Sink for 78 Days

beats.text: Fall into Jupiter from far away and you hit the clouds at about 57 kilometers per second.
beats.template_text: Fall into Jupiter from far away and you hit the clouds at about {{v_kms}} kilometers per second.
beats.spoken: Fall into Jupiter from far away and you hit the clouds at about fifty-seven kilometers per second.

beats.text: That is 57 times faster than a rifle bullet.
beats.template_text: That is {{x_rifle}} times faster than a rifle bullet.
beats.spoken: That is fifty-seven times faster than a rifle bullet.

beats.text: The air ahead of you turns into plasma as hot as the surface of the Sun.
beats.template_text: The air ahead of you turns into plasma as hot as the surface of the Sun.
beats.spoken: The air ahead of you turns into plasma as hot as the surface of the Sun.

beats.text: Every kilogram of you carries the energy of 390 kilograms of TNT.
beats.template_text: Every kilogram of you carries the energy of {{tnt_per_kg}} kilograms of TNT.
beats.spoken: Every kilogram of you carries the energy of three hundred and ninety kilograms of TNT.

beats.text: NASA's Galileo probe felt more than 200 g, behind a heat shield. The human record is 46.2 g.
beats.template_text: NASA's Galileo probe felt more than {{galileo_g}} g, behind a heat shield. The human record is {{stapp_g}} g.
beats.spoken: NASA's Galileo probe felt more than two hundred g, behind a heat shield. The human record is forty-six point two g.

beats.text: So you would not land on Jupiter. You would become a shooting star.
beats.template_text: So you would not land on Jupiter. You would become a shooting star.
beats.spoken: So you would not land on Jupiter. You would become a shooting star.

beats.text: Below Jupiter's cloud tops, there is a layer at room temperature.
beats.template_text: Below Jupiter's cloud tops, there is a layer at room temperature.
beats.spoken: Below Jupiter's cloud tops, there is a layer at room temperature.

beats.text: Up top it is 108 degrees below zero, at the 1 bar level.
beats.template_text: Up top it is {{c_1bar}} degrees below zero, at the 1 bar level.
beats.spoken: Up top it is one hundred and eight degrees below zero, at the one bar level.

beats.text: Fall through the white ammonia clouds, the rust-colored layer and the water clouds with their lightning.
beats.template_text: Fall through the white ammonia clouds, the rust-colored layer and the water clouds with their lightning.
beats.spoken: Fall through the white ammonia clouds, the rust-colored layer and the water clouds with their lightning.

beats.text: About 65 kilometers down, the air hits 20 degrees Celsius.
beats.template_text: About {{z_room}} kilometers down, the air hits {{room_c}} degrees Celsius.
beats.spoken: About sixty-five kilometers down, the air hits twenty degrees Celsius.

beats.text: NASA's Galileo probe logged it in 1995, about 30 minutes after entry.
beats.template_text: NASA's Galileo probe logged it in 1995, about {{room_min}} minutes after entry.
beats.spoken: NASA's Galileo probe logged it in nineteen ninety-five, about thirty minutes after entry.

beats.text: Comfortable, except there is no oxygen to breathe. Only hydrogen and helium.
beats.template_text: Comfortable, except there is no oxygen to breathe. Only hydrogen and helium.
beats.spoken: Comfortable, except there is no oxygen to breathe. Only hydrogen and helium.

shorts.title: Where you'd finally stop inside Jupiter

beats.text: Jupiter has no surface. So if you fell in, where would you finally stop?
beats.template_text: Jupiter has no surface. So if you fell in, where would you finally stop?
beats.spoken: Jupiter has no surface. So if you fell in, where would you finally stop?

beats.text: Not in the clouds. Those are only about 71 kilometers thick.
beats.template_text: Not in the clouds. Those are only about {{clouds_km}} kilometers thick.
beats.spoken: Not in the clouds. Those are only about seventy-one kilometers thick.

beats.text: Not at 1,000 kilometers, where it is about 1,900 degrees Celsius.
beats.template_text: Not at {{d1000}} kilometers, where it is about {{t1000_c}} degrees Celsius.
beats.spoken: Not at one thousand kilometers, where it is about one thousand nine hundred degrees Celsius.

beats.text: The hydrogen keeps getting denser, until about 14,000 kilometers down it is as dense as you.
beats.template_text: The hydrogen keeps getting denser, until about {{float_km}} kilometers down it is as dense as you.
beats.spoken: The hydrogen keeps getting denser, until about fourteen thousand kilometers down it is as dense as you.

beats.text: And there, you float, in hot, crushing hydrogen, under about 2 million atmospheres.
beats.template_text: And there, you float, in hot, crushing hydrogen, under about {{float_matm}} million atmospheres.
beats.spoken: And there, you float, in hot, crushing hydrogen, under about two million atmospheres.

beats.text: Getting there takes about 78 days. Jupiter never lets you touch it.
beats.template_text: Getting there takes about {{sink_days}} days. Jupiter never lets you touch it.
beats.spoken: Getting there takes about seventy-eight days. Jupiter never lets you touch it.

beats.text: You fall into Jupiter at 210,000 kilometers an hour, and there is no ground to stop you. So where do you actually stop?
beats.template_text: You fall into Jupiter at {{v_kmh}} kilometers an hour, and there is no ground to stop you. So where do you actually stop?
beats.spoken: You fall into Jupiter at two hundred and ten thousand kilometers an hour, and there is no ground to stop you. So where do you actually stop?

beats.text: Here are the rules. You start at rest, 1,000,000 kilometers from Jupiter's center, and you let go. No rocket, no parachute. Only gravity.
beats.template_text: Here are the rules. You start at rest, {{start_km}} kilometers from Jupiter's center, and you let go. No rocket, no parachute. Only gravity.
beats.spoken: Here are the rules. You start at rest, one million kilometers from Jupiter's center, and you let go. No rocket, no parachute. Only gravity.

beats.text: At first, nothing seems to happen. Jupiter is a striped coin hanging in the dark. But it is pulling, and the pull never lets go.
beats.template_text: At first, nothing seems to happen. Jupiter is a striped coin hanging in the dark. But it is pulling, and the pull never lets go.
beats.spoken: At first, nothing seems to happen. Jupiter is a striped coin hanging in the dark. But it is pulling, and the pull never lets go.

beats.text: For 27 hours you fall, while Jupiter spins about 2.7 times beneath you and swells to fill the sky. By the end you are moving at 57 kilometers per second. That is 57 times faster than a rifle bullet, and faster than NASA's Galileo probe, which hit this atmosphere at 47.4.
beats.template_text: For {{fall_h}} hours you fall, while Jupiter spins about {{fall_turns}} times beneath you and swells to fill the sky. By the end you are moving at {{v_kms}} kilometers per second. That is {{x_rifle}} times faster than a rifle bullet, and faster than NASA's Galileo probe, which hit this atmosphere at {{galileo_kms}}.
beats.spoken: For twenty-seven hours you fall, while Jupiter spins about two point seven times beneath you and swells to fill the sky. By the end you are moving at fifty-seven kilometers per second. That is fifty-seven times faster than a rifle bullet, and faster than NASA's Galileo probe, which hit this atmosphere at forty-seven point four.

beats.text: For scale: Jupiter is 11 Earths wide. The Great Red Spot alone, a storm, is about twice as wide as our whole planet.
beats.template_text: For scale: Jupiter is {{size_earths}} Earths wide. The Great Red Spot alone, a storm, is about twice as wide as our whole planet.
beats.spoken: For scale: Jupiter is eleven Earths wide. The Great Red Spot alone, a storm, is about twice as wide as our whole planet.

beats.text: And there is no ground. Jupiter has no surface at all. So on the way down we will track three things: how deep you are, how hot it is, and what you see out the window.
beats.retention: Sets the 3 recurring questions + open loop (where do you stop?)
beats.template_text: And there is no ground. Jupiter has no surface at all. So on the way down we will track three things: how deep you are, how hot it is, and what you see out the window.
beats.spoken: And there is no ground. Jupiter has no surface at all. So on the way down we will track three things: how deep you are, how hot it is, and what you see out the window.

beats.text: Then the air arrives, and not gently. At 57 kilometers per second even thin hydrogen hits like a wall. The gas ahead of you is crushed into glowing plasma, as hot as the surface of the Sun.
beats.template_text: Then the air arrives, and not gently. At {{v_kms}} kilometers per second even thin hydrogen hits like a wall. The gas ahead of you is crushed into glowing plasma, as hot as the surface of the Sun.
beats.spoken: Then the air arrives, and not gently. At fifty-seven kilometers per second even thin hydrogen hits like a wall. The gas ahead of you is crushed into glowing plasma, as hot as the surface of the Sun.

beats.text: Every kilogram of you carries the energy of about 390 kilograms of TNT. For a whole person, that is about 28 tonnes, released in moments.
beats.template_text: Every kilogram of you carries the energy of about {{tnt_per_kg}} kilograms of TNT. For a whole person, that is about {{tnt_you}} tonnes, released in moments.
beats.spoken: Every kilogram of you carries the energy of about three hundred and ninety kilograms of TNT. For a whole person, that is about twenty-eight tonnes, released in moments.

beats.text: Galileo survived this behind a heat shield and still felt more than 200 g. The most any human has survived on purpose is 46.2 g. Galileo took more than four times that.
beats.template_text: Galileo survived this behind a heat shield and still felt more than {{galileo_g}} g. The most any human has survived on purpose is {{stapp_g}} g. Galileo took more than four times that.
beats.spoken: Galileo survived this behind a heat shield and still felt more than two hundred g. The most any human has survived on purpose is forty-six point two g. Galileo took more than four times that.

beats.text: So honestly? You do not survive the entry. You become a meteor, a streak of light above the clouds. But this is The If Engine, so we cheat exactly once. Put yourself in an indestructible pod, your size and your weight. Everything outside it stays real.
beats.template_text: So honestly? You do not survive the entry. You become a meteor, a streak of light above the clouds. But this is The If Engine, so we cheat exactly once. Put yourself in an indestructible pod, your size and your weight. Everything outside it stays real.
beats.spoken: So honestly? You do not survive the entry. You become a meteor, a streak of light above the clouds. But this is The If Engine, so we cheat exactly once. Put yourself in an indestructible pod, your size and your weight. Everything outside it stays real.

beats.text: The pod slows to a fall you could almost call calm: about 690 kilometers an hour. The thicker the air, the slower you fall, and from here it only gets thicker.
beats.template_text: The pod slows to a fall you could almost call calm: about {{vt_1bar_kmh}} kilometers an hour. The thicker the air, the slower you fall, and from here it only gets thicker.
beats.spoken: The pod slows to a fall you could almost call calm: about six hundred and ninety kilometers an hour. The thicker the air, the slower you fall, and from here it only gets thicker.

beats.text: First rung. Depth: just above the 1 bar level, Jupiter's version of sea level. Temperature: about 120 degrees below zero. Out the window: white.
beats.template_text: First rung. Depth: just above the 1 bar level, Jupiter's version of sea level. Temperature: about {{c_nh3}} degrees below zero. Out the window: white.
beats.spoken: First rung. Depth: just above the one bar level, Jupiter's version of sea level. Temperature: about one hundred and twenty degrees below zero. Out the window: white.

beats.text: These high white clouds are ammonia ice, a snow made of the chemical in household cleaner, at about 0.70 bar. The winds up here reach 539 kilometers an hour.
beats.template_text: These high white clouds are ammonia ice, a snow made of the chemical in household cleaner, at about {{p_nh3}} bar. The winds up here reach {{wind_kmh}} kilometers an hour.
beats.spoken: These high white clouds are ammonia ice, a snow made of the chemical in household cleaner, at about zero point seven zero bar. The winds up here reach five hundred and thirty-nine kilometers an hour.

beats.text: Here is the first surprise. A study in 2025 suggests most of the color you see from space comes from deeper, from a rust-colored layer below this one. So let's go and look.
beats.retention: Tease: the colour comes from deeper
beats.template_text: Here is the first surprise. A study in 2025 suggests most of the color you see from space comes from deeper, from a rust-colored layer below this one. So let's go and look.
beats.spoken: Here is the first surprise. A study in twenty twenty-five suggests most of the color you see from space comes from deeper, from a rust-colored layer below this one. So let's go and look.

beats.text: Second rung. Depth: about 18 kilometers. Pressure: 2 bar, double the air on a beach on Earth.
beats.template_text: Second rung. Depth: about {{z_nh4sh}} kilometers. Pressure: {{p_nh4sh}} bar, double the air on a beach on Earth.
beats.spoken: Second rung. Depth: about eighteen kilometers. Pressure: two bar, double the air on a beach on Earth.

beats.text: Temperature: about 72 degrees below zero. These are crystals of ammonium hydrosulfide, stained by a haze the color of rust. The sunlight is fading fast.
beats.template_text: Temperature: about {{c_nh4sh}} degrees below zero. These are crystals of ammonium hydrosulfide, stained by a haze the color of rust. The sunlight is fading fast.
beats.spoken: Temperature: about seventy-two degrees below zero. These are crystals of ammonium hydrosulfide, stained by a haze the color of rust. The sunlight is fading fast.

beats.text: And somewhere below you, something flashes.
beats.template_text: And somewhere below you, something flashes.
beats.spoken: And somewhere below you, something flashes.

beats.text: Third rung. About 49 kilometers down, 5 bar, 12 degrees below zero and rising. These are water clouds. Real water ice and droplets, like the storms at home.
beats.template_text: Third rung. About {{z_h2o}} kilometers down, {{p_h2o}} bar, {{c_h2o}} degrees below zero and rising. These are water clouds. Real water ice and droplets, like the storms at home.
beats.spoken: Third rung. About forty-nine kilometers down, five bar, twelve degrees below zero and rising. These are water clouds. Real water ice and droplets, like the storms at home.

beats.text: And they are electric. NASA's Juno spacecraft found lightning even higher up, where it is 88 degrees below zero, fed by slushy hailstones of ammonia and water that scientists call mushballs.
beats.template_text: And they are electric. NASA's Juno spacecraft found lightning even higher up, where it is {{c_lightning}} degrees below zero, fed by slushy hailstones of ammonia and water that scientists call mushballs.
beats.spoken: And they are electric. NASA's Juno spacecraft found lightning even higher up, where it is eighty-eight degrees below zero, fed by slushy hailstones of ammonia and water that scientists call mushballs.

beats.text: All three cloud layers together are only about 71 kilometers thick. About 36 minutes after you passed the 1 bar level, you are already 100 kilometers down. You have fallen through Jupiter's entire weather.
beats.template_text: All three cloud layers together are only about {{clouds_km}} kilometers thick. About {{t100_min}} minutes after you passed the 1 bar level, you are already {{d100}} kilometers down. You have fallen through Jupiter's entire weather.
beats.spoken: All three cloud layers together are only about seventy-one kilometers thick. About thirty-six minutes after you passed the one bar level, you are already one hundred kilometers down. You have fallen through Jupiter's entire weather.

beats.text: Then the temperature does something strange.
beats.template_text: Then the temperature does something strange.
beats.spoken: Then the temperature does something strange.

beats.text: About 65 kilometers down, at 7.5 bar, the air outside is a comfortable 20 degrees Celsius.
beats.template_text: About {{z_room}} kilometers down, at {{p_room}} bar, the air outside is a comfortable {{room_c}} degrees Celsius.
beats.spoken: About sixty-five kilometers down, at seven point five bar, the air outside is a comfortable twenty degrees Celsius.

beats.text: When the Galileo probe reached this level in 1995, NASA logged it in its timeline: room temperature, about 30 minutes after entry.
beats.template_text: When the Galileo probe reached this level in 1995, NASA logged it in its timeline: room temperature, about {{room_min}} minutes after entry.
beats.spoken: When the Galileo probe reached this level in nineteen ninety-five, NASA logged it in its timeline: room temperature, about thirty minutes after entry.

beats.text: It is the most Earth-like moment of the whole trip, and you could not breathe for a second of it. There is no oxygen to breathe here, only hydrogen and helium.
beats.template_text: It is the most Earth-like moment of the whole trip, and you could not breathe for a second of it. There is no oxygen to breathe here, only hydrogen and helium.
beats.spoken: It is the most Earth-like moment of the whole trip, and you could not breathe for a second of it. There is no oxygen to breathe here, only hydrogen and helium.

beats.text: Galileo kept talking for 58 minutes. It sank about 160 kilometers. Then its signal stopped.
beats.template_text: Galileo kept talking for {{gal_min}} minutes. It sank about {{gal_km}} kilometers. Then its signal stopped.
beats.spoken: Galileo kept talking for fifty-eight minutes. It sank about one hundred and sixty kilometers. Then its signal stopped.

beats.text: Within about 10 hours, NASA estimates, the probe was completely vaporized. No working instrument has ever reported back from below this depth.
beats.template_text: Within about {{vapor_h}} hours, NASA estimates, the probe was completely vaporized. No working instrument has ever reported back from below this depth.
beats.spoken: Within about ten hours, NASA estimates, the probe was completely vaporized. No working instrument has ever reported back from below this depth.

beats.text: You keep sinking. Your pod is indestructible, remember. But from here, the question is not whether you survive. It is what is left of the sky.
beats.retention: Open loop: what is left of the sky
beats.template_text: You keep sinking. Your pod is indestructible, remember. But from here, the question is not whether you survive. It is what is left of the sky.
beats.spoken: You keep sinking. Your pod is indestructible, remember. But from here, the question is not whether you survive. It is what is left of the sky.

beats.text: Fourth rung. 1,000 kilometers down. The sunlight is long gone. Temperature: about 1,900 degrees Celsius. Pressure: around 8,000 atmospheres.
beats.template_text: Fourth rung. {{d1000}} kilometers down. The sunlight is long gone. Temperature: about {{t1000_c}} degrees Celsius. Pressure: around {{p1000_round}} atmospheres.
beats.spoken: Fourth rung. one thousand kilometers down. The sunlight is long gone. Temperature: about one thousand nine hundred degrees Celsius. Pressure: around eight thousand atmospheres.

beats.text: At that temperature the hull of your pod glows orange, like steel in a forge. Down here, heat is the only light there is.
beats.template_text: At that temperature the hull of your pod glows orange, like steel in a forge. Down here, heat is the only light there is.
beats.spoken: At that temperature the hull of your pod glows orange, like steel in a forge. Down here, heat is the only light there is.

beats.text: It took you about 21 hours to sink this far, and the gas is now so thick that you are falling at 27 kilometers an hour, the speed of a bicycle.
beats.template_text: It took you about {{t1000_h}} hours to sink this far, and the gas is now so thick that you are falling at {{v1000_kmh}} kilometers an hour, the speed of a bicycle.
beats.spoken: It took you about twenty-one hours to sink this far, and the gas is now so thick that you are falling at twenty-seven kilometers an hour, the speed of a bicycle.

beats.text: And somewhere around here, the line between gas and liquid simply disappears.
beats.template_text: And somewhere around here, the line between gas and liquid simply disappears.
beats.spoken: And somewhere around here, the line between gas and liquid simply disappears.

beats.text: There is no splash and no surface. The hydrogen just gets denser and denser until, without any line you could point to, it behaves like a liquid. NASA calls it the largest ocean in the solar system.
beats.template_text: There is no splash and no surface. The hydrogen just gets denser and denser until, without any line you could point to, it behaves like a liquid. NASA calls it the largest ocean in the solar system.
beats.spoken: There is no splash and no surface. The hydrogen just gets denser and denser until, without any line you could point to, it behaves like a liquid. NASA calls it the largest ocean in the solar system.

beats.text: Fifth rung. Thousands of kilometers deep, sinking slower every hour. Jupiter's jet streams reach down about 3,200 kilometers. You are already below them.
beats.template_text: Fifth rung. Thousands of kilometers deep, sinking slower every hour. Jupiter's jet streams reach down about {{jets_km}} kilometers. You are already below them.
beats.spoken: Fifth rung. Thousands of kilometers deep, sinking slower every hour. Jupiter's jet streams reach down about three thousand two hundred kilometers. You are already below them.

beats.text: And then, about 14,000 kilometers down, you stop.
beats.retention: Payoff of the hook: where you stop
beats.template_text: And then, about {{float_km}} kilometers down, you stop.
beats.spoken: And then, about fourteen thousand kilometers down, you stop.

beats.text: Not because you hit anything. The liquid around you is now as dense as you are, so you float, like a swimmer who stopped kicking, in a sea of hot, crushing hydrogen, under about 2 million atmospheres.
beats.template_text: Not because you hit anything. The liquid around you is now as dense as you are, so you float, like a swimmer who stopped kicking, in a sea of hot, crushing hydrogen, under about {{float_matm}} million atmospheres.
beats.spoken: Not because you hit anything. The liquid around you is now as dense as you are, so you float, like a swimmer who stopped kicking, in a sea of hot, crushing hydrogen, under about two million atmospheres.

beats.text: That is the answer to the question from the start. Jupiter has no ground, so what stops you is buoyancy. In a simple model of Jupiter's interior, you come to rest about 20 percent of the way to the center.
beats.template_text: That is the answer to the question from the start. Jupiter has no ground, so what stops you is buoyancy. In a simple model of Jupiter's interior, you come to rest about {{float_pct}} percent of the way to the center.
beats.spoken: That is the answer to the question from the start. Jupiter has no ground, so what stops you is buoyancy. In a simple model of Jupiter's interior, you come to rest about twenty percent of the way to the center.

beats.text: Getting here took about 78 days. You crossed 1,000,000 kilometers of space in 27 hours, then spent 78 days sinking the last 14,000.
beats.template_text: Getting here took about {{sink_days}} days. You crossed {{start_km}} kilometers of space in {{fall_h}} hours, then spent {{sink_days}} days sinking the last {{float_km}}.
beats.spoken: Getting here took about seventy-eight days. You crossed one million kilometers of space in twenty-seven hours, then spent seventy-eight days sinking the last fourteen thousand.

beats.text: And below you, out of reach, is the strangest layer. NASA thinks that perhaps halfway to the center, hydrogen is squeezed so hard that it turns into a liquid metal, and its churning powers Jupiter's enormous magnetic field.
beats.template_text: And below you, out of reach, is the strangest layer. NASA thinks that perhaps halfway to the center, hydrogen is squeezed so hard that it turns into a liquid metal, and its churning powers Jupiter's enormous magnetic field.

beats.text: Deeper still, NASA's Juno found that the core is not a solid ball. It is dilute, partly dissolved, with no clear edge. Even at the very bottom, Jupiter refuses to have a floor.
beats.template_text: Deeper still, NASA's Juno found that the core is not a solid ball. It is dilute, partly dissolved, with no clear edge. Even at the very bottom, Jupiter refuses to have a floor.
beats.spoken: Deeper still, NASA's Juno found that the core is not a solid ball. It is dilute, partly dissolved, with no clear edge. Even at the very bottom, Jupiter refuses to have a floor.

beats.text: So here is the twist. You set out to fall into Jupiter, and you never touched it. No surface at the top, no floor at the bottom. Just a world that gets thicker and thicker, until it holds you, suspended, in the dark.

alt_titles: What Happens If You Fall Into Jupiter?
You Fall Into Jupiter at 210,000 km/h. Where Do You Stop?
metadata.hook: What if you fell into Jupiter? Falling into Jupiter from 1 million km, you hit the clouds at 210,000 km/h, then sink through every layer inside Jupiter: ammonia, rust-colored and water clouds, past the depth where NASA's Galileo probe went silent, into an ocean of hydrogen. Jupiter has no surface, so where do you actually stop?
learn: How fast you hit Jupiter if you fall from far away, and how long the fall takes
Why an unprotected entry is fatal, compared with NASA's Galileo probe
Jupiter's three cloud layers, its lightning and its room-temperature level
What lies below the deepest point any probe has reached
Where you finally stop inside a planet with no surface, and why
key_numbers: Arrival speed from 1 million km: about 57 km/s after 27 hours of falling
Entry energy: about 390 kg of TNT for every kilogram of you
Galileo probe: more than 200 g on entry, data for 58 minutes
Room temperature about 65 km below the 1-bar level (simple adiabat model)
Neutral buoyancy about 14,000 km down, after about 78 days of sinking (index-1 polytrope model)
metadata.assumptions: Assumptions: you start at rest 1,000,000 km from Jupiter's centre; after the entry you ride an indestructible human-sized pod with the density of a human body. Upper atmosphere: ideal-gas dry adiabat (about); interior: index-1 polytrope (a simple model). Depths are measured below the 1-bar level. Layer boundaries in the cutaway are schematic.
